name: Shanenawa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.

new_statements.quote: Como observamos nos dados expostos, em (54), independente do número de sílabas de que a palavra é constituída, o acento é sempre predizível, caindo de forma recorrente na última sílaba. Os dados em (54:i-l) ainda nos mostram que o acréscimo de afixos não interfere na posição do acento que permanece recaindo na sílaba final. (pp. 45-46) [...] (61) Regra do acento primário - Atribua um asterisco à sílaba pesada final. (p. 48) [...] Nesses termos, em Shanenawa, o acento não é contrastivo, ou seja, a sílaba proeminente não é usada para distinguir palavras formalmente idênticas, embora apresente sentidos diversos. Em suma, o acento tem caráter apenas demarcativo. (p. 49)
new_statements.translation: As we observe in the data set out in (54), regardless of the number of syllables the word is made of, stress is always predictable, falling recurrently on the last syllable. The data in (54:i-l) further show us that the addition of affixes does not interfere with the position of the stress, which keeps falling on the final syllable. (pp. 45-46) [...] (61) Primary stress rule - Assign an asterisk to the final heavy syllable. (p. 48) [...] In these terms, in Shanenawa stress is not contrastive, that is, the prominent syllable is not used to distinguish formally identical words with different meanings. In sum, stress has a merely demarcative character. (p. 49)
new_statements.citation: Cândido, Gláucia Vieira (2004). Descrição Morfossintática da Língua Shanenawa. Campinas, SP: UNICAMP. Universidade Estadual de Campinas. xxvi+264 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog final stress (fixed final) is exactly what Cândido 2004 states; the work adds that stress is non-contrastive/demarcative, that the final syllable is always heavy (closed, glottal stop insertion) so the author frames it as quantity-sensitivity that always picks the final syllable, that affixation does not move stress, and that compounds show secondary prominence on non-final members.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the last syllable of every word, regardless of syllable count and regardless of suffixation; monosyllables are all stressed (p. 45, ex. 54). Cândido formalises this with Hayes (1995) as non-iterative right-to-left binary right-headed feet with End Rule Right (exx. 55-57), but then argues the fixed final placement is really quantity-sensitivity: word-final syllables are systematically heavy (closed by /N/, a coronal, /j/, /w/, or, phonetically, by an inserted glottal stop [ʔ] which she treats as the physical correlate of stress), so the rule is 'assign the asterisk to the final heavy syllable' (p. 47-48). Stress is non-contrastive and purely demarcative (p. 49); the Conclusão (p. 221) restates the language as one with traditionally 'fixed stress', always on the last syllable, hence not a distinctive feature. She notes the same final-stress pattern in Kaxinawá (Camargo 1991) and Katukina (Aguiar 1994).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only in compounds: each non-final member keeps a weaker prominence on its own final syllable (its final glottal stop is dropped), while the absolute final syllable of the compound carries primary stress, e.g. [i«viʔ pa»niʔ] 'cama', [ta«Riʔ ci»Siʔ] 'calça', [pi«aʔ na»waʔ] 'espingarda' (pp. 47-48, exx. 58-59). Stress also serves as a word-boundary cue: one prominence per phonological word (ex. 60, p. 48; sec. on the phonological word, p. 41 and ch. III).
new_statements.exceptions: None lexical. Monosyllables (rare) are all stressed (p. 45). The author expresses doubt (p. 46) that Hayes's foot parameters genuinely apply, preferring the weight account; the final-heaviness of every word is the only conditioning mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: Cândido 2004 describes the Shanenawa of the Katukina/Kaxinawá indigenous land on the Envira river, Município de Feijó, Acre (Brazil), four communities: Morada Nova, Paredão, Cardoso, Nova Vida (pp. 1-4 of the thesis); fieldwork centred on the Morada Nova village. No dialect split is claimed. Cândido notes final stress is shared with Kaxinawá and Katukina (p. 46), other Panoan languages, not this language.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed final' (final stress) rests on Cândido 2004, the standard and only reference description of Shanenawa (UNICAMP PhD, 264 pp, with a 27-page stress section), corroborated by the same author's 1998 phonology MA. Both were open-access but not yet obtained; both downloaded now to The record's quotation is verbatim at sec. 2.1.4 p.45-46 and Conclusions p.221. Both sources state stress is exceptionlessly word-final, non-contrastive, unaffected by affixation, with compound-internal secondary stress on the left member; the 2004 'quantity-sensitive' wording is analytic only (every word-final syllable is closed), as the record's cite note already says. No competing or later phonological/instrumental study exists (Glottolog n=2, web search nil). Action: fill the empty cite/loc/grade fields with 'Cândido 2004: 45-46, 48 (rule 61), 221

sources.quote: p.97: 'Os dados em (28) evidenciam que nessa língua, à exceção dos monossilábicos, o acento recai sempre sobre a última sílaba das palavras simples. tone.quote: Quanto ao acento primário, este tem caráter apenas demarcativo, ou seja, não é contrastivo (CÂNDIDO, 2004). Além disso, é sempre previsível, pois, independente do número de sílabas de que a palavra é constituída, cai sempre na última sílaba, a qual é sempre pesada. [...] Neste artigo, verificamos que a língua Shanenawa apresenta acento secundário nas palavras compostas e mantém, como acontece nas palavras simples (primitivas), o acento primário na última sílaba. Em tal processo, constatamos um tipo de determinação morfológica para o acento secundário, pois o acento primário da primeira palavra primitiva dentro do composto é mantido como acento secundário.
tone.locator: sec. 2, p. 109 (first part); sec. 6 Conclusão, p. 113 (second part; p. 114 holds only the end of the conclusion and the references)
tone.translation: As for primary stress, it is merely demarcative, i.e. not contrastive (Cândido 2004). Moreover it is always predictable since, regardless of the number of syllables in the word, it always falls on the last syllable, which is always heavy. [...] In this article we found that Shanenawa has secondary stress in compound words and keeps, as in simple (primitive) words, primary stress on the last syllable. In this process we found a kind of morphological determination of secondary stress, since the primary stress of the first primitive word inside the compound is kept as secondary stress.
